# And because of the difference of characteristics (2.4.19)

## 2.4.19

There is also a difference in characteristics between the Chief Breath and the others. When speech and the other organs are asleep, the Chief Breath alone remains awake. That Breath alone is not reached by death, while the others are reached by it. Through its staying and departing, it alone is the cause of the preservation and fall of the physical body, not the sense-organs. Furthermore, the cause of perceiving sense-objects belongs to the sense-organs, not to the Chief Breath. In this manner, there is a very great distinction of characteristics between the vital breath and the sense-organs. For this reason too, their status as distinct entities is established. 

As for what was said—that according to the scriptural passage, 'All of them became of the same form as this one' <note>original: "ta etasyaiva sarve rūpamabhavan" from Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21</note>, the senses are indeed the breath itself—that is improper. Even in that passage, difference is recognized upon examining the preceding and following context. To explain: having enumerated the senses such as speech with the passage, 'Speech held: "I shall indeed keep speaking"', the text states that speech and the rest were seized by death in the form of fatigue: 'Death, having become fatigue, seized them; therefore speech indeed grows weary'. Having thus declared that speech and the others were seized by death in the form of fatigue, it separately enumerates the Breath as not overcome by death: 'Now it did not reach this one who is the central breath'. It also affirms its superiority with the statement, 'This one indeed is the greatest among us'. Therefore, without contradicting that context, one must consider that the phrase 'becoming of its form' means that speech and the other senses depend on the Chief Breath for obtaining their movement, not that they share absolute identity of essence. 

For this very reason, the secondary <note>metaphorical or figurative</note> application of the word <term>prāṇa</term> <gloss>breath</gloss> to the sense-organs is established. And thus scripture shows the secondary usage of the word <term>prāṇa</term>, whose primary sense belongs to the Chief Breath, in reference to the sense-organs: 'All of them became of the same form as this one; therefore they are named after this one as breaths'. Therefore, the senses such as speech are entities distinct from the Chief Breath.

# But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to the One who makes them threefold, because of scriptural teaching (2.4.20)

## Section on the Fashioning of Names and Forms (2.4.20)

In the context of the True Being <note>the creation narrative in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad</note>, after stating the creation of fire, water, and food, scripture teaches: 'That divinity conceived: "Well, let Me enter these three divinities with this living self and differentiate names and forms. Let Me make each one of them threefold, threefold"' <note>original: "seyaṃ devataikṣata hantāhamimāstisro devatā anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇīti. tāsāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtamekaikāṃ karavāṇīti" from Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2-3</note>. 

Here arises a doubt: Is this differentiation of names and forms the action of the individual soul, or is it the action of the Supreme Lord?

On this point, the opposing view initially presents itself: This differentiation of names and forms must be the action of the individual soul alone. Why? Because of the qualifying phrase 'with this living self' <note>original: "anena jīvenātmanā"</note>. Just as in ordinary life, in a statement such as 'Having entered the enemy army through a spy, let me assess it', the king attributes the assessment of the army to himself using the first-person expression 'let me assess', even though the action is actually done by the spy, because the king is the instigating agent; so too, although the differentiation of names and forms is actually performed by the individual soul, the divinity attributes it to Himself using the first-person expression 'let Me differentiate', because He is the instigating agent. Moreover, in conventional names like Dittha and Davittha, and in physical forms like clay pots and dishes, it is observed that the individual soul alone is the differentiator. From this, the conclusion would seem to follow that this differentiation of names and forms is done by the individual soul alone.

In response to this, the author states: 'But the fashioning of names and forms...' The word 'but' turns aside this objection. 'The fashioning of names and forms' means the differentiation of names and forms. 'Belongs to the One who makes them threefold' points to the Supreme Lord, because His unreserved agency is taught in the threefold division. This fashioning of names and forms—such as fire, sun, moon, and lightning, or among grasses, reeds, and palāśa trees, or among beasts, wild animals, and human beings, manifold in every species and in every individual—can indeed be the work only of the Supreme Lord who created fire, water, and earth. 

Why? Because of scriptural teaching. For scripture teaches the agency of the Supreme Brahman alone, beginning with 'That divinity' and continuing with the first-person verb 'let Me differentiate'. 

If one objects: 'Is it not established from the qualifying phrase "with the living self" that the agency belongs to the individual soul?'—that is not so. The phrase 'with the living self' is connected with the verb 'having entered', because of immediate proximity, and not with 'let Me differentiate'. If it were connected with the latter, the first-person expression 'let Me differentiate' referring to the divinity would have to be understood figuratively. Furthermore, the powerless individual soul does not possess the capacity to fashion diverse names and forms such as mountains, rivers, and oceans. Even in those matters where the individual soul has capacity, that capacity is entirely dependent upon the Supreme Lord. Nor is the individual soul entirely separate from the Supreme Lord—like a spy from a king—because of the qualifying word 'self', and because the individual condition is caused merely by limiting adjuncts. Therefore, even the differentiation of names and forms performed by the soul is ultimately performed by the Supreme Lord alone.

# And Because of the Difference in Characteristics (2.4.19)

## 2.4.19

There is also a difference in characteristics between the Chief Breath and the others. When speech and the other organs are asleep, the Chief Breath alone remains awake. It alone is not overtaken by death, whereas the others are overtaken. Through its staying and departing, it alone is the cause of the body's sustenance and fall, not the sensory organs. The sensory organs are the cause of perceiving sense objects, not the Chief Breath. In this manner, there is an extensive distinction in characteristics between the vital breath and the senses. For this reason as well, their status as distinct principles is established.

As for what was stated, that according to the scriptural passage, "They all became forms of this very Breath" <note>original: "ta etasyaiva sarve rūpamabhavan" from Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21</note>, the senses are identical to the Breath, that is incorrect. Even there, an examination of the preceding and succeeding context reveals a distinction. For instance, after reciting speech and the other senses, saying, "Speech resolved: 'I shall indeed speak'" <note>original: "vadiṣyāmyevāhamiti vāgdadhre"</note>, the text declares that speech and the rest were seized by death in the form of fatigue: "Death, taking the form of weariness, overtook them; therefore speech indeed grows weary" <note>original: "tāni mṛtyuḥ śramo bhūtvopayeme tasmācchrāmyatyeva vāk"</note>. It then introduces the Breath separately, showing it was untouched by death: "Then it could not reach this one, who is the central breath" <note>original: "athaimameva nāpnodyo'yaṃ madhyamaḥ prāṇaḥ"</note>. It also establishes its preeminence by stating, "This one is indeed the greatest among us" <note>original: "ayaṃ vai naḥ śreṣṭhaḥ"</note>.

Therefore, to avoid contradiction with that passage, the statement that the senses became forms of the Chief Breath must be understood as meaning that speech and the other organs depend on the Breath for their vital movement, not that they share absolute identity with it. Precisely for this reason, the use of the word "breath" <note>original: "prāṇa"</note> for the senses is proven to be figurative. And so the scripture indicates the figurative application of the word "breath" to the sense organs, which primarily designates the Chief Breath: "They all became forms of this very Breath. Therefore, they are called by its name, 'the breaths'" <note>original: "ta etasyaiva sarve rūpamabhavan, tasmādeta etenākhyāyante prāṇāḥ"</note>. Therefore, speech and the other sensory organs are distinct principles from the Chief Breath.

# But the Fashioning of Names and Forms Belongs to Him Who Makes Tripartite, on Account of Teaching (2.4.20)

## Section on the Fashioning of Names and Forms (2.4.20)

In the discussion on the True Reality, having described the creation of fire, water, and food, scripture teaches: "That Deity thought: 'Indeed, having entered these three deities with this living individual self, let Me differentiate names and forms. Let Me make each one of them threefold'" <note>original: "seyaṃ devataikṣata hantāhamimāstisro devatā anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇīti, tāsāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtamekaikāṃ karavāṇīti" from Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2-3</note>.

On this point, there is a doubt: Does this differentiation of names and forms have the individual soul as its agent, or does it have the Supreme Lord as its agent?

The initial view suggests: This differentiation of names and forms belongs strictly to the individual soul. Why? Because of the qualifying phrase "with this living individual self" <note>original: "anena jīvenātmanā"</note>. In worldly usage, in expressions such as "Having entered the enemy army through a spy, let me count it," even though the actual counting of the army is performed by the spy, the king attributes the action to himself as the directing agent by using the first-person verb "let me count." Similarly, even though the differentiation of names and forms is performed by the individual soul, the Deity attributes the action to Himself as the instigator, using the first-person verb "let Me differentiate" <note>original: "vyākaravāṇi"</note>. Moreover, in names such as Dittha and Davittha <note>conventional Sanskrit placeholder names, like John Doe and Jane Doe</note>, and in forms such as clay pots and shallow dishes, agency in differentiation is observed to belong to the living soul alone. Therefore, the differentiation of names and forms belongs to the soul.

In response to this objection, the author declares: "But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him Who makes tripartite, on account of teaching." The word "but" turns aside the opposing view. "Fashioning of names and forms" means the manifestation and diversification of names and physical shapes. "To Him Who makes tripartite" designates the Supreme Lord, because scripture attributes the agency of triplication unconditionally to Him. This fashioning of names and physical forms, such as fire, the sun, the moon, and lightning, as well as various kinds among grasses such as <term>kuśa</term> <gloss>sacred sacrificial grass</gloss>, <term>kāśa</term> <gloss>wild thatch grass</gloss>, and <term>palāśa</term> <gloss>flame-of-the-forest tree</gloss>, and among animals, wild beasts, and humans, differentiated in manifold ways according to genus and individual, can only be the work of the Supreme Lord, who is the creator of fire, water, and earth.

Why? Because of direct scriptural teaching. Beginning with "That Deity," and using the first-person form "let Me differentiate," scripture teaches that agency in differentiation belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone.

If it is objected that because of the qualification "with the living self," agency in differentiation is determined to belong to the soul, we reply: that is not so. The words "with the living self" connect with "having entered," due to proximity in the sentence, not with "let Me differentiate." For if connected with the latter, the first-person verb "let Me differentiate," which refers to the Deity, would have to be interpreted figuratively.

Furthermore, an unempowered individual soul does not possess the capacity to fashion varied and vast names and forms such as mountains, rivers, and oceans. Even in cases where the soul does possess capacity, that capacity is entirely dependent upon the Supreme Lord. Nor is the individual soul utterly different from the Supreme Lord, like a spy from a king, because of the qualifying word "as Myself" <note>original: "ātmanā"</note>, and because the state of individuality is caused merely by limiting adjuncts <note>original: "upādhi"</note>. Therefore, even the differentiation of names and forms carried out by the soul is ultimately performed by the Supreme Lord alone.

# And because of the difference of characteristics (2.4.19)

## 2.4.19

There is also a difference in characteristic between the Chief Breath and the others. When speech and the rest are asleep, the Chief Breath alone remains awake. It alone is untouched by death, whereas the others are overtaken by it. By its remaining and departing alone, the maintenance and fall of the body are caused, not by the senses. And the sensory organs are the causes of perceiving sense objects, not the Chief Breath. Such is the great difference of characteristics between the Chief Breath and the senses. For this reason too, their status as distinct realities is established. 

As for what was argued that speech and the others are identical with the Breath on account of the scripture saying, 'They all assumed its form' <note>original: "te etasyaiva sarve rūpam abhavan" from Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21</note>, that is not valid. Even in that passage, distinction is understood when one considers what precedes and follows. For instance, having enumerated speech and the other senses with the passage, 'Speech resolved: I will indeed speak,' and having declared that speech and the rest were overtaken by death in the form of fatigue with the words, 'Death took possession of them in the form of weariness; therefore speech grows weary,' the scripture goes on to state separately that this Breath was not overcome by death: 'Now, death did not reach this one who is the middle breath.' It then affirms its preeminence: 'This one is indeed the best among us.' Therefore, so as not to contradict that passage, speech and the others having the form of Breath means that their acquisition of movement depends upon the Breath, not that there is an absolute identity of essence. 

For this very reason, the use of the word <term>prāṇa</term> <gloss>breath</gloss> with reference to the senses is figurative. Thus the scripture demonstrates this figurative usage of the word <term>prāṇa</term>, which properly belongs to the Chief Breath, when applied to the senses: 'They all assumed its form; therefore they are named after it as the breaths.' Therefore, speech and the other senses are distinct realities from the Chief Breath.

# But the fashioning of name and form belongs to the one who makes threefold, because of instruction (2.4.20)

## Section on the Fashioning of Name and Form (2.4.20)

In the section concerning Being <term>sat</term> <gloss>the ultimate Reality</gloss>, after stating the creation of fire, water, and earth, it is taught: 'That Divinity glanced: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living individual self and evolve names and forms. Let me make each one of them threefold, threefold"' <note>original: "seyaṃ devataikṣata hantāham imās tisro devatā anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇīti | tāsāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtam ekaikāṃ karavāṇīti" from Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2-3</note>. 

Here a doubt arises: Does this manifestation of name and form have the individual self <term>jīva</term> <gloss>individual living soul</gloss> as its agent, or does it have the Supreme Lord <term>parameśvara</term> <gloss>the Supreme Ruler</gloss> as its agent? 

On this matter, the prima facie view holds that this manifestation of name and form belongs to the individual self alone. Why? Because of the qualification 'with this living individual self.' Just as in common worldly speech, in an expression such as 'Having entered the enemy's army through a spy, let me count them,' the counting of the army is performed by the spy, but the king attributes it to himself using the first person 'let me count' because he is the instigating agent; even so, although the differentiation of names and forms is performed by the individual self, the Divinity attributes it to itself using the first person 'let me differentiate' because it is the instigating cause. Moreover, in the case of names such as Dittha and Davittha, and forms such as a pot and a dish, the agency of differentiation is observed to belong to the living individual self alone. Therefore, when it is thus proposed that this manifestation of names and forms belongs to the individual self alone:

The Sutra replies: 'But the fashioning of name and form.' The word 'but' turns away the opposing position. 'Fashioning of name and form' means the differentiation of name and form. 'Belongs to the one who makes threefold' designates the Supreme Lord, because the scriptural instruction assigns to Him the undisputed agency in making the elements threefold. This fashioning of names and fashioning of forms, such as fire, sun, moon, and lightning, and likewise among grasses, reeds, and palāśa trees, and among cattle, wild beasts, and human beings, manifold in every species and in every individual, can surely be the work only of the Supreme Lord, the creator of fire, water, and earth. Why? Because of the instruction. For beginning with 'That Divinity,' the agency of differentiation is taught here to belong to the Supreme Brahman alone by the use of the first person 'let me differentiate.' 

If it is objected that because of the qualification 'with the living individual self,' the agency of differentiation is determined to belong to the individual soul, that is not so. The words 'with the living individual self' connect with 'having entered' on account of proximity, not with 'let me differentiate.' For if connected with the latter, the first person 'let me differentiate' referring to the Divinity would have to be understood figuratively. Furthermore, the individual soul, not being the Lord, lacks the power to differentiate manifold names and forms such as mountains, rivers, and oceans. Even where it does possess such power, that power is entirely dependent on the Supreme Lord. Nor is the individual soul fundamentally different from the Supreme Lord, like a spy from a king, because of the specification 'with myself' and because the condition of being an individual soul is based merely on limiting adjuncts <term>upādhi</term> <gloss>conditioning superimpositions</gloss>. Therefore, even the differentiation of names and forms performed by the individual soul is ultimately performed by the Supreme Lord alone.
